blocks.text: A supermarket freezer cabinet holds food at about -20 °C in a shop at 25 °C. Heat leaks in all day, and a small sealed circuit of refrigerant, a compressor, two heat exchangers and a valve pumps it back out. How much electricity does that pumping cost per kilowatt of cooling? That ratio is the coefficient of performance, and this unit shows how to calculate it.

blocks.markdown: A refrigerator moves heat $Q_L$ from a cold space to a warm surrounding. The second law says this needs work input, so we use a working fluid (the **refrigerant**) that boils at a low temperature in the cold space and condenses at a higher temperature in the warm surroundings. Boiling absorbs a large latent heat; condensing rejects it. A compressor raises the pressure so that the condensing temperature is above the surroundings.

blocks.title: Ideal vapour-compression cycle
blocks.text: Four steady-flow processes: 1-2 isentropic compression of saturated vapour; 2-3 constant-pressure heat rejection in the condenser to saturated liquid; 3-4 throttling at constant enthalpy; 4-1 constant-pressure heat absorption in the evaporator to saturated vapour. Kinetic and potential energy changes are neglected.

blocks.caption: Property bookkeeping for the ideal cycle.

blocks.markdown: Applying the steady-flow energy equation to each component (per unit mass of refrigerant, no heat or work except where stated) gives the three quantities we need: the **refrigerating effect** $q_L$, the **specific compressor work** $w_{in}$ and the **coefficient of performance**.

blocks.latex: q_L = h_1 - h_4 = h_1 - h_3 \qquad w_{in} = h_2 - h_1 \qquad \mathrm{COP}_R = \frac{q_L}{w_{in}} = \frac{h_1-h_4}{h_2-h_1}
blocks.caption: Units: h in kJ/kg, so q and w are in kJ/kg; COP is dimensionless.
Mass flow rate $\dot m$ in kg/s gives powers in kW.

blocks.title: COP of an ideal R-134a cycle
blocks.prompt: An ideal vapour-compression cycle uses R-134a between 0.14 MPa (evaporator) and 0.8 MPa (condenser). Use these typical tabulated values (rounded): at 0.14 MPa saturated vapour $h_1 = 239.16$ kJ/kg; isentropic compression to 0.8 MPa gives $h_2 \approx 275.39$ kJ/kg; saturated liquid at 0.8 MPa has $h_3 = 95.47$ kJ/kg. Find the refrigerating effect, compressor work and COP.

steps.text: State 4 is reached by throttling, so $h_4 = h_3 = 95.47$ kJ/kg.
Refrigerating effect is the enthalpy rise through the evaporator.
Compressor work is the enthalpy rise across the isentropic compressor.

blocks.answer: q_L = 143.69 kJ/kg, w_in = 36.23 kJ/kg, COP = 3.97. About four units of cooling per unit of electrical work.

blocks.title: Compressor power for a given cooling load
blocks.prompt: A cold store needs a cooling load of 12 kW. The ideal cycle runs with representative (approximate) R-134a values $h_1 = 244.5$ kJ/kg, $h_2 = 272.0$ kJ/kg and $h_3 = 88.8$ kJ/kg. Find the refrigerant mass flow rate, compressor power and COP.

steps.text: Refrigerating effect per kg, with $h_4 = h_3$.
Mass flow from the cooling load.

blocks.answer: m = 0.0771 kg/s, compressor power = 2.12 kW, COP = 5.66 (check: 12/2.12).

blocks.markdown: **Why a throttle valve and not a turbine?** An ideal reversible cycle would expand the high-pressure liquid through a turbine to recover work. In practice the fluid leaving the condenser is a dense liquid, so expansion work is tiny (the specific volume is small and barely changes at first). As pressure falls the liquid flashes and a two-phase mixture forms, which erodes blades and gives poor turbine efficiency. A valve or capillary tube is cheap, has no moving parts and gives accurate control of flow, at the cost of a small loss of refrigerating effect.

blocks.title: What the valve does
blocks.text: Throttling is an irreversible constant-enthalpy process, $h_4 = h_3$, with entropy generation. The refrigerating effect is reduced by the quality-driven flash at state 4, because that vapour fraction has already boiled without absorbing heat from the cold space.

items: Lower evaporator pressure: lower $T_L$, larger pressure ratio, higher compressor work, lower COP.
Higher condenser pressure: smaller refrigerating effect and larger compressor work, lower COP.
Compressor power scales with the mass flow rate $\dot m$, which is set by the cooling load.
The cycle COP can exceed 1 because heat is moved, not created.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Do not read $h_4$ from the saturated-vapour column at the evaporator pressure: $h_4 = h_3$ comes from the condenser-side liquid enthalpy. Do not divide by $h_2 - h_3$ (that is the condenser heat, used for heat-pump COP). Keep $q$ in kJ/kg and $\dot Q$ in kW distinct.

points: Refrigerating effect: $q_L = h_1 - h_4$ with $h_4 = h_3$.
Compressor work $w_{in} = h_2 - h_1$ and $\mathrm{COP}_R = q_L / w_{in}$.
Cooling load fixes the mass flow, which then fixes compressor power.
A throttle valve replaces the turbine because liquid expansion yields little work and two-phase expansion is impractical.

questions.stem: A turbine is NOT normally used to expand the refrigerant between the condenser and evaporator of a domestic refrigerator. Which is the best reason?

options.text: A turbine would raise the refrigerant temperature above the condensing temperature
Throttling is reversible so it gives the highest possible COP
Expansion of a dense liquid recovers very little work and flashing into a two-phase mixture is hard on a turbine, whereas a valve is simple and cheap
The second law forbids any work output from a refrigerant expansion

questions.correctOptionText: Expansion of a dense liquid recovers very little work and flashing into a two-phase mixture is hard on a turbine, whereas a valve is simple and cheap

distractorRationale.a: Expansion lowers the temperature; this misstates the physics.
distractorRationale.b: Throttling is irreversible; it is chosen for practicality, not efficiency.
distractorRationale.d: Expansion work is allowed by the second law; it is simply small and impractical to recover.

questions.explanation: The refrigerant leaves the condenser as a liquid of small specific volume, so the recoverable expansion work is only a small fraction of compressor work. Flashing to a two-phase mixture also erodes turbine blades, so a throttling valve is used.

questions.stem: The coefficient of performance of an ideal vapour-compression refrigerator is defined as

options.text: heat absorbed in the evaporator divided by compressor work input
compressor work input divided by heat absorbed in the evaporator
heat rejected in the condenser divided by compressor work input
compressor work divided by heat rejected in the condenser

questions.correctOptionText: heat absorbed in the evaporator divided by compressor work input

distractorRationale.b: This is the inverse of the COP.
distractorRationale.c: That is the heat-pump COP, not the refrigerator COP.
distractorRationale.d: This is not a standard performance measure.

questions.explanation: A refrigerator is rated on the benefit it delivers, which is cooling $q_L = h_1 - h_4$, divided by the cost, which is work $w_{in} = h_2 - h_1$. The heat-pump COP instead uses the condenser heat $h_2 - h_3$ in the numerator.

questions.stem: An ideal cycle has $h_1 = 236.0$ kJ/kg (saturated vapour leaving the evaporator) and $h_3 = 98.0$ kJ/kg (saturated liquid leaving the condenser). What is the refrigerating effect?

options.text: 334.0 kJ/kg
236.0 kJ/kg
98.0 kJ/kg
138.0 kJ/kg

distractorRationale.a: Adds the enthalpies instead of subtracting.
distractorRationale.b: Uses $h_1$ alone and ignores the throttling state.
distractorRationale.c: Uses $h_3$, the condenser-exit liquid, not the enthalpy difference.

questions.explanation: Throttling is isenthalpic, so $h_4 = h_3 = 98.0$ kJ/kg. The refrigerating effect is $h_1 - h_4 = 236.0 - 98.0 = 138.0$ kJ/kg.

questions.stem: Refrigerant at 1.2 MPa is saturated liquid with enthalpy 117 kJ/kg and passes through an expansion valve to the evaporator pressure. What is the enthalpy at the valve exit, assuming steady flow, negligible heat loss and no change in velocity?

options.text: Lower than 117 kJ/kg, because the pressure drops
117 kJ/kg
Higher than 117 kJ/kg, because the liquid absorbs heat from the cold space
Equal to the saturated-vapour enthalpy at the evaporator pressure

distractorRationale.a: Pressure drop does not reduce enthalpy; the energy balance gives equal enthalpies.
distractorRationale.c: Heat absorption happens later, in the evaporator, not in the valve.
distractorRationale.d: That is state 1 after the evaporator, not the valve exit.

questions.explanation: With no work, negligible heat transfer and no change in kinetic energy, the steady-flow energy equation reduces to $h_{in} = h_{out}$. Part of the liquid flashes to vapour at the expense of its own sensible energy, so the temperature falls while the enthalpy stays 117 kJ/kg.

questions.stem: Two ideal cycles share the same evaporator with $h_1 = 240.0$ kJ/kg. Cycle A: $h_2 = 270.0$, $h_3 = 100.0$ kJ/kg (lower condensing pressure). Cycle B: $h_2 = 282.0$, $h_3 = 115.0$ kJ/kg (higher condensing pressure). Which statement is correct?

options.text: Cycle B has the larger COP because it compresses to a higher pressure
Both cycles have the same COP because they share $h_1$
Cycle A has COP 4.67 and Cycle B has COP 2.98, so A is more efficient
Cycle A has COP 2.98 and Cycle B has COP 4.67, so B is more efficient

questions.correctOptionText: Cycle A has COP 4.67 and Cycle B has COP 2.98, so A is more efficient

distractorRationale.a: Higher pressure means more work and a smaller refrigerating effect, so COP falls.
distractorRationale.b: COP depends on $h_2$ and $h_3$ as well.

questions.explanation: Cycle A: $q_L = 140$, $w = 30$ kJ/kg, COP = 4.67. Cycle B: $q_L = 125$, $w = 42$ kJ/kg, COP = 2.98. A higher condensing pressure reduces the refrigerating effect and increases the compressor work, so COP falls.

questions.stem: An ideal vapour-compression cycle has evaporator exit enthalpy $h_1 = 235.3$ kJ/kg and condenser exit (saturated liquid) enthalpy $h_3 = 101.6$ kJ/kg. Find the refrigerating effect in kJ/kg.
questions.explanation: Throttling gives $h_4 = h_3 = 101.6$ kJ/kg. The refrigerating effect is $h_1 - h_4 = 235.3 - 101.6 = 133.7$ kJ/kg.

questions.stem: A small cold room has a cooling load of 8.0 kW. The ideal cycle uses representative values $h_1 = 235.3$ kJ/kg, $h_2 = 272.0$ kJ/kg and $h_3 = 101.6$ kJ/kg. Calculate the compressor power in kW.
questions.explanation: Refrigerating effect is $235.3 - 101.6 = 133.7$ kJ/kg, so $\dot m = 8.0/133.7 = 0.0598$ kg/s. Compressor work is $272.0 - 235.3 = 36.7$ kJ/kg, so $\dot W = 0.0598 \times 36.7 = 2.20$ kW.

questions.stem: A fault-finding engineer records the ideal cycle states of a chiller as $h_1 = 246.0$ kJ/kg, $h_2 = 277.0$ kJ/kg and $h_3 = 105.0$ kJ/kg. Calculate the COP (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: Refrigerating effect is $246.0 - 105.0 = 141.0$ kJ/kg and compressor work is $277.0 - 246.0 = 31.0$ kJ/kg. COP $= 141.0/31.0 = 4.548$.

questions.stem: A student proposes replacing the throttle valve of an ideal vapour-compression refrigerator with a turbine to raise the COP. Explain whether this is thermodynamically beneficial and why it is rarely done.
markingGuide: States that an expander would lower $h_4$ and so increase the refrigerating effect $h_1 - h_4$ (beneficial in principle)
Notes the recovered work would also offset compressor work
Explains that liquid has small specific volume so expansion work is a small fraction of compressor work
Notes two-phase flashing flow harms turbine blades and efficiency
Notes cost, complexity, small size and control advantages of valve or capillary tube
Concludes that the small gain does not justify the cost
questions.explanation: An expander would deliver work and lower $h_4$, but the gain is small because liquids are nearly incompressible. Practical issues of two-phase flow, cost and control dominate, so a valve is used.

questions.stem: An ideal vapour-compression cycle works between an evaporating temperature of -10 °C and a condensing temperature of 40 °C, and has a COP of 4.5. A Carnot refrigerator between the same temperatures would have COP 5.26. Explain why the vapour-compression COP is lower, naming at least three sources of irreversibility or departure from Carnot in the ideal cycle.
markingGuide: Throttling is irreversible and replaces a work-producing expansion
Compression of vapour ends in superheat, so some heat rejection occurs above the condensing temperature
Finite temperature differences in the evaporator and condenser (refrigerant temperatures differ from the reservoirs)
Links the lower COP to larger work for the same refrigerating effect
questions.explanation: The Carnot COP between 263.15 K and 313.15 K is 5.26. The cycle falls below it because of throttling, desuperheating of compressor discharge vapour and finite temperature differences.
